heuristics.rule: If you have research publications and citations, pursue EB-1B or EB-2 NIW before defaulting to employer-sponsored EB-2
heuristics.condition: When a China-born applicant in tech/academia has a measurable publication or citation record...
heuristics.action: Seriously evaluate EB-1B (Outstanding Researcher) or EB-2 NIW as primary GC strategy rather than waiting for employer PERM
heuristics.because: EB-1 China backlog is significantly shorter than EB-2 China, and EB-1B/NIW paths exist independently of PERM labor certification timelines

heuristics.rule: EB-1A is the only employment-based category that does not require employer sponsorship or PERM
heuristics.condition: When an applicant wants to avoid dependency on a single employer during a multi-year GC process...
heuristics.action: Pursue EB-1A (Extraordinary Ability) self-petition if qualifications allow, bypassing PERM entirely
heuristics.because: EB-1A has no employer sponsorship requirement and no PERM process, and as of 2024 EB-1A China priority dates are significantly ahead of EB-2 India/China

heuristics.rule: For India-born applicants, treat Canada PR as a parallel track rather than a fallback
heuristics.condition: When an India-born applicant faces EB-2 India wait times exceeding their career planning horizon...
heuristics.action: Begin Express Entry preparation concurrently with US H-1B employment rather than waiting to see if US GC resolves
heuristics.because: EB-2 India priority date as of 2024 is ~2012, implying 50+ year wait for new filers; Canada Express Entry has delivered PR in ~14 months for comparable profiles

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Green card backlog is determined by country of birth, not current nationality. India and China-born applicants face drastically longer queues under the 7% per-country annual cap.
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify your country of birth and look up the current USCIS Visa Bulletin priority date for your birth country and target EB category

decision_factors.factor: EB category eligibility (EB-1 vs EB-2 vs EB-3)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: EB-1 has a dramatically shorter backlog than EB-2 for both China and India-born applicants. Qualifying for EB-1 can shorten wait time by decades.
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Evaluate publication record, citations, awards, peer review history for EB-1B; evaluate national interest argument for EB-2 NIW

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Company acquisition, closure, or layoff can interrupt a PERM-based GC application mid-process, requiring restart of the labor certification process
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Assess company financial health, acquisition risk, and whether your role is likely to exist in 3-5 years

decision_factors.factor: Career planning time horizon vs. backlog wait time
decision_factors.why_it_matters: If the expected GC wait exceeds a person's intended US career duration or retirement horizon, the GC process may never complete within their active career
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Compare current priority date movement rate against your filing year to estimate realistic approval year; compare to personal career timeline

decision_factors.factor: Willingness to accept salary reduction for PR certainty in Canada
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Canada PR via Express Entry is achievable in ~14 months but often involves a ~25% salary reduction vs. US tech salaries
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Model net compensation after cost of living adjustment; evaluate personal tolerance for salary vs. status security tradeoff

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Staying on H-1B while waiting for EB-2 India GC
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The wait can exceed an entire career span. Children born in the US become citizens while the parent remains on H-1B for 15+ years. The psychological cost of indefinite status uncertainty compounds over time.
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: India-born applicants who entered the EB-2 queue in the 2010s or later; anyone who assumed the GC process was a formality rather than a multi-decade commitment

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Changing employers during an active PERM-based GC process
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Changing jobs requires restarting the PERM labor certification process with the new employer, which can partially or fully reset the GC timeline depending on priority date portability eligibility
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: H-1B holders who want career mobility but have an active GC filing, particularly those early in the process without an approved I-140

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing Canada over the US for immigration certainty
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Realizing the psychological cost of indefinite US visa status only after years of H-1B renewals; the salary reduction (~25%) may be offset by lower stress, but this tradeoff is not apparent until experienced firsthand
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: High-earning US tech workers who prioritize status security over maximum compensation, particularly after experiencing H-1B renewal anxiety repeatedly

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating GC sponsorship as a routine HR process rather than a multi-decade personal commitment
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Employers frame PERM filing as a standard benefit, and early in a career the wait times feel abstract and distant; the backlog only becomes viscerally real years later
failure_patterns.consequence: Applicants reach mid-career still on H-1B, with limited job mobility, career decisions constrained by GC status, and no clear resolution date
warning_signs: Applicant cannot state their current priority date or what year it maps to in expected approval
Applicant assumes they can freely change jobs without GC impact
Applicant has not researched EB-1 eligibility despite years of professional experience

failure_patterns.pattern: Defaulting to EB-2 employer-sponsored path without evaluating EB-1 eligibility
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Employers default to EB-2 PERM because it is their standard process; applicants rarely initiate an independent EB-1 assessment unless specifically advised
failure_patterns.consequence: Years lost in a slower queue when EB-1B or EB-1A may have been achievable, resulting in a 10-20 year difference in expected approval
warning_signs: Applicant has peer-reviewed publications or citations but has never discussed EB-1B with an immigration attorney
Applicant assumes the employer's chosen GC path is the only or best path

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your current priority date, and what year does the USCIS Visa Bulletin suggest that date will become current?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the applicant has a realistic understanding of their actual GC timeline, or is operating on vague optimism
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you modeled what your career and life situation will look like in that year? Does it still make sense to wait?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: You need to look this up immediately — many people discover their realistic approval year is after their planned retirement

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have peer-reviewed publications, significant citations, or other evidence of outstanding research contributions?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether EB-1B (Outstanding Researcher) or EB-2 NIW is a realistic alternative to employer-sponsored EB-2, potentially shortening the wait by decades
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you had an immigration attorney assess your EB-1B eligibility? EB-1 China dates are significantly ahead of EB-2 China.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Are you building toward those qualifications, or does your profile fit EB-1A (Extraordinary Ability) in another dimension?

diagnostic_questions.question: If your employer closed or was acquired tomorrow, what happens to your GC process?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the applicant understands PERM portability rules and has an I-140 approved, which is the key threshold for job change flexibility
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Is your I-140 approved? If yes, you may have portability rights after 180 days in a similar role.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: You are fully dependent on this employer for your GC path — this is a significant concentration risk that should factor into career decisions

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you seriously modeled what a Canada Express Entry path would look like for your profile?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the applicant is anchored on the US path by inertia rather than by genuine comparison of outcomes
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What is your CRS score estimate, and have you compared the expected timeline and salary tradeoff explicitly?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: For India-born applicants especially, this comparison is essential given EB-2 India timelines — not running this analysis is a form of decision avoidance

industry_realities.common_belief: H-1B is a temporary visa and the GC process is just a formality you complete on the way to permanent status
industry_realities.actual_reality: For India-born applicants, EB-2 India priority dates as of 2024 are ~2012, meaning new filers face an estimated 50+ year wait. The GC process is not a formality — it is a multi-decade commitment with no guaranteed outcome within a career lifespan.
industry_realities.implication: India-born applicants should treat EB-2 as essentially inaccessible and immediately evaluate EB-1, NIW, or alternative country paths

industry_realities.common_belief: You can freely change jobs while your GC is in process
industry_realities.actual_reality: Changing employers before I-140 approval typically requires restarting the PERM labor certification with the new employer. After I-140 approval and 180+ days, portability may apply — but only to similar roles and only if the priority date is preserved.
industry_realities.implication: Job mobility decisions must be coordinated with GC stage; changing jobs at the wrong stage can cost years of queue position

industry_realities.common_belief: EB-1A requires a Nobel Prize-level achievement and is not realistic for most people
industry_realities.actual_reality: EB-1A (Extraordinary Ability) has a high bar but is self-petitioned with no employer sponsorship and no PERM process. For China-born applicants, EB-1A priority dates are significantly shorter than EB-2, making it worth a serious eligibility assessment even for strong-but-not-famous professionals.
industry_realities.implication: Applicants should get a formal EB-1A eligibility assessment from an experienced immigration attorney rather than self-disqualifying based on perceived bar

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Assumes that filing for GC means it will eventually come through in a reasonable timeframe; treats 'my company is sponsoring my GC' as equivalent to 'I will get a GC'
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Immediately looks up current priority date for their birth country and EB category, calculates realistic approval year, and stress-tests their career plan against that timeline
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Acting on the naive assumption leads to a decade or more of career decisions (job loyalty, geographic choices, life planning) made on a false premise

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Accepts whatever GC path the employer initiates (typically EB-2 PERM) without independently evaluating EB-1 eligibility
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Proactively evaluates EB-1B, EB-1A, and EB-2 NIW options independently of employer default, understanding that employer convenience and applicant optimization are not the same thing
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The difference between EB-1 and EB-2 for China/India-born applicants can be 10-30 years of wait time

junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Treats US GC as the only valid immigration goal; views Canada PR as a consolation prize or last resort
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Models Canada Express Entry as a parallel track with concrete timeline (14 months achievable), and explicitly trades off salary reduction against status certainty and psychological cost of indefinite H-1B status
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Failing to model the Canada path means making the US-stay decision by default rather than by comparison, which is a form of decision avoidance with major long-term consequences

community_misconceptions.misconception: The 7% per-country cap is based on citizenship, so if you naturalized or hold a passport from another country, you can use a shorter queue
community_misconceptions.why_believed: People conflate nationality/citizenship with country of birth; many immigrants hold multiple passports or have changed citizenship
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: The per-country cap is based on country of birth, not citizenship or current nationality. A China-born person with Canadian citizenship still files under the China-born quota.
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Applicants who believe they can 'escape' the backlog via naturalization elsewhere are wrong and may waste years on a strategy that does not work

community_misconceptions.misconception: H-1B can only be renewed a limited number of times, so you must get GC before you 'run out' of H-1B
community_misconceptions.why_believed: H-1B is nominally a 6-year visa (3+3), and many people believe there is a hard cap after which you must leave
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: H-1B can be extended beyond the initial 6 years in 1-year or 3-year increments once a GC application has been pending for 365+ days (under AC21). In practice, people with active GC filings can remain on H-1B indefinitely while waiting.
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Applicants may make premature or panicked decisions (accepting worse jobs, rushing GC steps) based on a false belief that their H-1B will expire before GC approval

real_case_outcomes.situation: India-born engineer filed EB-2 India in 2009 while on H-1B; continued working in the US at the same employer
real_case_outcomes.decision: Stayed on H-1B waiting for GC through the standard EB-2 India queue
real_case_outcomes.outcome: As of 2024 (15 years later), still waiting. Children born in the US are US citizens. The parent remains on H-1B with no clear resolution date.
real_case_outcomes.lesson: For India-born applicants, EB-2 India is not a viable GC strategy for anyone filing after approximately 2008-2010. The wait exceeds most people's career horizons. Alternative paths (EB-1, Canada PR) must be evaluated early.

real_case_outcomes.situation: China-born professional on H-1B in the US for 7 years; had active GC filing but no near-term resolution
real_case_outcomes.decision: Relocated to Canada and applied via Express Entry
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Received Canada PR in 14 months. Accepted ~25% salary reduction. Reports significantly lower psychological stress.
real_case_outcomes.lesson: Canada Express Entry is a realistic 12-18 month path to permanent status for qualified professionals. The salary tradeoff is real (~25%) but the psychological cost of indefinite H-1B status is also real and often underweighted in the US-vs-Canada decision.

psychological_barriers.trigger: An applicant who has been on H-1B for 5+ years with an active GC filing asks whether they should 'just wait it out' because they've already invested so much time
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Sunk cost fallacy — years already spent in the US GC queue feel like an investment that must be protected, making it psychologically difficult to evaluate alternative paths on their current merits
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Reluctance to seriously model Canada or other alternatives; framing the question as 'how much longer do I need to wait' rather than 'what is the optimal decision now given current information'
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe: 'The years you've spent do not change what happens from today forward. If you filed EB-2 India today, you'd wait until the 2070s. The question is not how to honor past investment — it's what path maximizes your next 20 years.'

psychological_barriers.trigger: Applicant frames the GC backlog as a problem they need to 'solve' or 'fix' rather than a structural reality they need to plan around
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Illusion of control — believing that finding the right trick, attorney, or category will resolve what is fundamentally a supply/demand problem baked into US immigration law
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Excessive research into obscure GC strategies; asking 'is there any way to speed this up' repeatedly without acting on the answers; paralysis from information overload
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Name the structural reality directly: 'There is no trick. The backlog is real. Your decision is whether to wait, pursue EB-1 if eligible, or exit to Canada. All three are valid. Paralysis is the only truly bad choice.'

psychological_barriers.trigger: India or China-born applicant asks whether they should stay in the US or go to Canada, framing it as a quality-of-life question
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Avoidance of the core fear: that the US GC may never come, which would mean years of H-1B were 'wasted' — so the person avoids making the comparison explicit
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Asking about abstract lifestyle factors (weather, culture, salary) rather than directly comparing immigration status timelines; seeking permission to leave rather than making a decision
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Force the timeline comparison: 'Write down the year you expect to get a US GC. Write down the year you'd get Canada PR. Now decide.' The comparison, made concrete, usually resolves the paralysis.

reframing_moves.original_framing: How long will I have to wait for my green card? (asked as if seeking reassurance or a manageable number)
reframing_moves.reframe: The question is not how long you will wait — it is whether the wait fits inside your career and life planning horizon at all
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Shifts from a passive waiting mindset to an active planning mindset; forces the applicant to confront whether the GC is actually a viable goal given their specific situation rather than an abstract eventual outcome
reframing_moves.example_language: If you filed EB-2 India today, your expected approval year is in the 2070s. Does that fit your plan?

reframing_moves.original_framing: Should I go to Canada or stay in the US and wait for my GC? (framed as a values/lifestyle tradeoff)
reframing_moves.reframe: This is not a lifestyle question — it is an immigration timeline question. Map both timelines concretely first, then decide.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: Removes the emotional weight from a decision that has a largely quantitative answer; most people who do the concrete timeline comparison find the decision becomes clearer
reframing_moves.example_language: One path gives you PR in 14 months. The other gives you PR in 40+ years. That's the actual comparison. Everything else is secondary.
